title: Israel's memorial and independence days
hook: Yom HaZikaron honors the fallen, then Yom HaAtzmaut follows; communities worldwide mark them very differently, and some not at all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom HaShoah: candles, a siren and names. Your line was remember in silence. A week later come two more days, side by side.

A flag hangs at half-mast on a hill in Jerusalem. All day, families have stood at military cemeteries across Israel, by the graves of sons and daughters, brothers, parents. The radio has played only quiet songs. Then the sun goes down, and in a single ceremony the flag is raised to the top of the pole, torches are lit, and fireworks go up. Some who stood at the graves that morning will be at a barbecue the next afternoon. A day of grief, a day of joy, and one sunset between them.
screen: `A FLAG AT HALF-MAST.` → `ONE SUNSET, THEN FIREWORKS.` → `BACK TO BACK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The first day is Yom HaZikaron, the day of remembrance, on the fourth of the Hebrew month of Iyar. It honors Israel's fallen soldiers and, in later years, civilians killed in attacks too. A siren sounds in the evening, and again the next morning. The second day is Yom HaAtzmaut, Independence Day, on the fifth of Iyar, marking the declaration of the State of Israel in May 1948. When either day would touch Shabbat, the dates move. The calendar puts them back to back on purpose: the ceremony that closes the first day opens the second. Memory first, then celebration. Inside Israel and outside it, Jews mark these days very differently. Some communities hold memorial services and festive gatherings. In religious Zionist synagogues, the psalms of praise called Hallel are often said on Independence Day, and some Reform and Conservative congregations have added readings for it. Haredi communities generally don't mark the days as religious occasions, and a few Haredi groups oppose the state on religious grounds. Some secular Israelis celebrate with no prayers at all, just flags and picnics. And for Palestinians, the same events of 1948 are remembered as the Nakba, the catastrophe. Today isn't about which view is right. It's about what's there: a pair of days, one of grief and one of joy, held by Jews in many different ways, and by some not at all.
screen: `YOM HAZIKARON: THE FALLEN.` · `YOM HAATZMAUT: MAY 1948.` · `ONE SUNSET BETWEEN THEM.` · `MANY WAYS, AND SOME NOT AT ALL.` · then, large: `MEMORY BEFORE CELEBRATION.`

segments.voice: Think of a community you know, your own synagogue, a friend's family, a city in Israel or abroad, and wonder what they might do on these two days. Then think of a time in your own life when a loss and a celebration came close together, and let both be true at once: grief, a sunset, then joy.
Yom HaZikaron. The day of remembrance: Israel's memorial day for its fallen, which gives way at sunset to Yom HaAtzmaut, Independence Day.
Your line: memory before celebration. The joy comes after the memory, not instead of it. That's day six hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: In Israel, Yom HaZikaron is marked with sirens and ceremonies at military cemeteries, and Yom HaAtzmaut begins at nightfall with a torch-lighting ceremony; Jewish communities elsewhere mark the days in many ways, some with added prayers such as Hallel, and some not at all.
